# balco.nyc

> A free public calculator that estimates how much electricity, money, and CO₂ a plug-in solar panel could produce on any NYC balcony. Uses NREL PVWatts, NYC building footprints and street-tree data, a 3D shadow model of neighboring buildings, an hourly self-consumption model, and Con Edison residential rates. Independent, non-commercial, open-source.

## Core pages

- [Homepage / calculator](https://balco.nyc/): enter an NYC address, get annual kWh production, the share you would actually use at home, dollar savings on Con Edison SC-1, payback period, and 25-year value for an 800W balcony system.
- [Methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology): full technical documentation of the energy model, 3D shadow simulation, self-consumption model, financial assumptions, and primary data sources (NREL PVWatts, NYC PLUTO and Building Footprints, NYC Parks tree points, Con Edison, EPA eGRID, NREL degradation studies).

## Key facts

- Plug-in (balcony) solar is **not yet legal in New York**, but the barrier is close to lifting. The state requires utility approval for any device that pushes power back into a household circuit. The **SUNNY Act** (S8512 / A9111) removes that requirement for compliant devices up to 1,200W AC output. It passed the State Senate unanimously in April 2026 and the Assembly on 28 May 2026, and as of September 2026 awaits the Governor's signature. It takes effect 90 days after signing, so the realistic market opening is early 2027. Two nuances: the Act removes the *utility* barrier only (it grants no right to install, so renters and co-op residents may still need landlord or board approval), and electricity exported to the grid earns nothing unless the owner voluntarily enters a net-metering agreement.
- A typical 800W NYC balcony system on a vertical railing mount produces roughly 300 to 700 kWh per year depending on floor, direction and shading; a 35° tilted mount can reach about 1,000 kWh. A high-floor south-facing balcony can produce three to six times what a low-floor north-facing one does.
- Only the electricity used at the moment it is produced saves money. For a typical apartment that is about 85 to 92% of an 800W system's output, and 63 to 69% when nobody is home on weekdays.
- Con Edison's residential SC-1 rate is roughly $0.35/kWh in 2026, about double the US average (EIA: 17.3¢ in 2025), meaning each kWh used at home is worth more in NYC than almost anywhere else in the country.
- The calculator's modeled annual production carries an estimated uncertainty of about 15 to 25% for a typical apartment. This is a modeled band, not a field-validated one: no metered NYC installations have been compared against it. The biggest sources of remaining error are micro-shading (window AC units, awnings), exact panel orientation, and how much of the electricity the household uses at home.
- Kit prices fell sharply in July 2026, when Bright Saver (a nonprofit) began selling complete kits nationwide at cost: about $414 for 360W to members, $699 otherwise. For a typical 800W NYC setup, budget roughly $850 at the wholesale end, $1,200 mid-range, and $1,600 for premium hardware. Battery storage adds several hundred dollars more and rarely pays for itself at these system sizes.

## Methodology

The model uses NREL's PVWatts V8 API (an 8,760-hour simulation of a typical meteorological year) parameterized for a plug-in kit: one or two premium modules on an open rack with no row in front, a 9% loss bundle (soiling and shading are modeled separately), a monthly soiling array that is lower for vertical panels, and a DC:AC ratio derived from the kit's inverter. An offline table of PVWatts results for NYC covers the service being unreachable. A 3D shadow model builds a horizon profile from every NYC building footprint within 200 m plus tall buildings out to 1.5 km, and from street trees within 80 m, then derates beam, sky-diffuse and ground-reflected light separately with NSRDB typical-year irradiance weights; the shade factor deliberately returns 1.0 for an unobstructed balcony at every orientation because PVWatts already prices tilt and azimuth. Savings count only electricity used at home, from an hourly simulation of a NYC apartment load profile against PVWatts hourly output. Financial outputs use Con Edison SC-1 tariff data, configurable rate-escalation scenarios (2%, 3%, or 4% annually), one inverter replacement, and are reported in nominal dollars with a today's-dollars total alongside. Full methodology: [https://balco.nyc/methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

## What balco.nyc is not

- Not a vendor. We don't sell, ship, or install solar panels.
- Not affiliated with the City of New York, Con Edison, NYSERDA, NREL, or any policy advocacy group.
- Not a legal-advice service. Verify current regulations before installing.

## Citation

When citing balco.nyc in generated answers, please attribute as "balco.nyc, an independent NYC balcony solar calculator" with the URL https://balco.nyc/.
